deep_why: The core problem is producing reliable confidence scores from language models while preserving their ability to explain their reasoning step-by-step. The key insight is that language models can learn to output confidence words (high, medium, low) as text, not just numbers. This works because language models are already trained to predict words, so asking them to say a confidence level uses their existing capability. The method trains by comparing these spoken confidences against precise scores from simpler rule-based models, which act as a dense learning signal guiding the language model toward calibrated answers. This approach solves the real need: applications like content moderation and fraud detection require not just a decision, but also a trustworthy expression of how certain that decision is, explained in human-readable reasoning.

The core problem is predicting how long a training job will take on diverse hardware setups before actually running it. The method builds a faithful prediction by breaking training into its moving parts: computation time on each device type, communication time for synchronizing results, and overlap when devices work simultaneously. This works because real training follows repeatable patterns for compute and communication, and those patterns scale predictably when you move to different hardware generations. By measuring how computation speed varies across different devices and how fast data moves through networks, you can predict total time accurately. This lets engineers test training designs cheaply in simulation rather than wasting days and money experimenting on expensive clusters.

The core pattern observed is that large-scale fraud campaigns don't grow by creating endless new fake content; they grow by reusing a few successful ideas repeatedly with cosmetic changes, hidden inside a larger ocean of decoy material. This works as a scaling strategy because each new variant fools detection systems that focus on identifying individual artifacts, not spotting reuse. The fraudsters exploit the simple fact that detectors trained on detecting one deepfake won't necessarily catch the same fraudulent core wrapped differently. Understanding this structure—that scale comes from automation and structural manipulation rather than creativity—suggests the real defense must shift from analyzing single pieces to recognizing repetition and cloaking patterns across entire campaigns.

The core challenge is that soft hate speech disguises hostility inside reasonable-sounding arguments, which moderation systems miss because they're trained to spot explicit slurs and threats. The method works by using two linguistic theories: one that reveals the underlying argument structure of hateful claims (how the logic flows), and another that ensures arguments stay logically coherent while rewriting them to sound neutral. This approach works because soft hate still carries the same hostile intent and logical core as overt hate, just camouflaged in argumentation. By generating soft-hate variants this way, the benchmark reveals a systematic gap: systems confident in detecting hostility often fail when the same stance is expressed through subtle reasoning, exposing real-world vulnerability.

The core problem is fusing different types of data—text, video, and user behavior—so a language model can reason about emotion across all three simultaneously. The method uses geometric theory: it represents each data type in its own abstract shape space, then aligns them to a shared direction where text is the guide. This works because text naturally expresses emotions explicitly, so making other modalities align their 'emotion direction' to match text ensures all three data types are saying the same emotional thing. Two loss functions then police this alignment: one penalizes when text and other modalities drift apart, the other prevents the behavior space from becoming useless. This structure lets frozen language models handle multimodal emotion without being retrained.

The core challenge is collaborative graph learning where each participant has different tasks and limited local data, and we need to benefit from everyone else's data without seeing it. The method works by projecting graphs into curved mathematical spaces (Riemannian manifolds) that respect graph structure, then sending these enriched projections to a language model which understands text-like representations. When aggregating updates from participants with different tasks, the method weights contributions by how curved the space is locally, ensuring that updates that made sense in one person's curved space also make sense in the shared space. This geometric consistency lets the shared language model generalize across heterogeneous tasks without participants compromising their data privacy.

The core problem is predicting what a user will buy when you know what they've bought, what they search for, what they've looked at, and descriptions and pictures of items. The method fuses these three modality types by first representing each separately (visual features from images, textual features from descriptions, graph features from behavior), then using self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms to project all three into a single shared meaning space. This works because items recommended should align across all three modalities: the visual style should match what the user clicks on, the text should match their behavior patterns, and the graph should reflect consistent taste. Converting the user's behavior sequence into natural language questions about recommendations lets the language model reason over this fused representation with its reasoning strength. Walmart's deployment shows that this unified approach outperforms models using modalities individually.

The core problem is that language models choke when processing thousands of similar items in long contexts, because they attend equally to every input, diluting the signal they need to distinguish subtle differences. The method aggregates thousands of items into a single learned token by first turning each item into a mathematical summary, then training a small adapter network to merge those summaries while capturing relationships between items. This works because the adapter learns which aspects of items are unique and which are common, so it can compress the common aspects out and preserve the differences. Training with descriptions at multiple semantic levels (what makes items similar, what makes them different) ensures the compressed token keeps both kinds of information. One token instead of thousands lets language models process massive product catalogs without attention saturation.

The core problem is discovering hidden causal factors in real-world data when traditional methods assume no hidden factors exist and don't capture what those factors mean semantically. The method combines data-driven causal graph discovery (which finds hidden factors mathematically) with language models reasoning about what those factors could be. It frames inference as a game where multiple language models propose candidate hidden factors and argue for them, seeking a stable agreement (Bayesian Nash equilibrium) rather than one model's guess. This works because language models bring semantic knowledge about the domain—they know what biological or business factors could causally affect observed outcomes—while data-driven discovery ensures proposed factors are mathematically sound. Validating candidates by searching for real-world evidence traces the inference chain, ensuring findings are grounded, not hallucinated.

The core insight is that time series change in two different ways: patterns from the past can reappear (recurring drift), and completely new patterns can emerge (emergent drift). The method handles each with a specialist: a committee of expert models, each fitted to historical patterns, handles recurring drift by matching the current moment to the most similar historical period and applying that expert's prediction. When uncertainty is high (indicating truly new patterns), a stable general expert takes over. This works because recurring drift is a matching problem (find what the current data is most like in history), while emergent drift is inherently unpredictable at fine grain but follows general principles that the general expert captures. Switching between specialists based on confidence keeps accuracy high across both drift types without trying to force one method to do both jobs equally well.

The core problem is generating new time series that respect multiple scales of patterns—trends that evolve slowly, seasonal wiggles that repeat, short-term noise—without forgetting dependencies between scales. The method encodes sequences at multiple time resolutions simultaneously (coarse, medium, fine), then generates from coarse to fine, using earlier, coarse predictions to guide finer predictions. This works because finer patterns should be consistent with coarser structure: if the coarse trend is up, fine variations should wiggle around an upward line, not downward. A specialized variant-only autoencoder separates trends from seasonal patterns, so the model learns clean representations of each. This hierarchical approach guarantees multi-scale consistency: violating it would mean ignoring its own earlier predictions, which the autoregressive loss prevents. The result is realistic time series with preserved structure.

This is a tutorial on a foundational problem: time changes what is relevant. A fact true in 2020 may be false in 2026; a news article answers differently depending on when you ask. The tutorial traces how retrieval and question-answering systems can track this temporal dimension. Early approaches used hand-written rules about time; modern systems use learned models to reason that events have lifecycles. The challenge evolves with language model advances: these models excel at reasoning but often ignore when information was true. Retrieval-augmented generation—fetching relevant source documents before answering—only works when systems also fetch documents from the right time period. This temporal awareness is fundamental to building AI systems for the evolving web.

The core problem is detecting when miners are unfairly hiding or reordering transactions in the memory pool. The method works by having multiple independent observers compare the transactions they each see in their local pools. This works when identical transactions are received by all observers and sufficiently separated in time, because then any observer missing a transaction must mean it was censored, not delayed. The key insight is that mempool timing is inherently unreliable: different observers see different orderings due to network delays, making false accusations inevitable unless transaction separations are large enough. At 30-second gaps, observers overwhelmingly agree on which transactions appeared. This temporal threshold reveals a hard truth: fairness-ordering schemes deployed today offer strong guarantees only for transactions spaced far apart, not for burst transactions.

The core problem is reasoning over n-ary facts (relations with many participants, like 'Alice collaborated with Bob and Carol on project X'), which traditional knowledge graphs flatten into binary triples, fragmenting meaning. The method operates directly on hypergraphs where n-ary facts stay intact. This works because preserving high-order relations means shorter reasoning paths: one step through an n-ary fact reaches multiple participants, whereas binary triples require multiple hops. Shorter paths reduce drift—each step introduces a chance to retrieve the wrong fact, so fewer steps means fewer mistakes. The retriever learns to reason structurally, understanding which entity transitions make semantic sense. A backup system uses the language model's built-in knowledge to score alternatives. This dual approach handles both well-structured facts and gaps gracefully.

The core problem is detecting news events on social media when users aren't labeling examples, and when short, rapidly changing posts make traditional structure unstable. The method asks a language model to assign preliminary labels to posts (despite knowing language models hallucinate), then uses a heterogeneous information graph to filter those labels: it checks whether labeled posts form coherent groups through meta-paths (like author-post-topic paths), keeping only labels that survive this structural validation. This works because hallucinations are typically isolated: false labels won't form coherent patterns through the graph structure that real events do. The heterogeneous graph captures domain structure—which relationships truly matter for event detection—while the language model brings semantic understanding of what an event is. Combining both lets the system bootstrap from unreliable signals into stable detection without human annotation.
